cards.claim: Increasing batch size maintains per-epoch accuracy when noise scale is preserved, without hyperparameter tuning
cards.conditions: SGD, SGD with momentum, Nesterov momentum, Adam on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet; constant number of training epochs
cards.effect: Test accuracy equivalent to learning rate decay schedule; fewer parameter updates (e.g., 29000→6500 on CIFAR-10, 14000→6000 on ImageNet)
cards.evidence: Experimental demonstration on CIFAR-10 (16-4 Wide ResNet) and ImageNet (Inception-ResNet-V2); three training schedules produce near-identical test curves when epoch budget is fixed
cards.quote: It is common practice to decay the learning rate. Here we show one can usually obtain the same learning curve on both training and test sets by instead increasing the batch size during training. This procedure is successful for stochastic gradient descent (SGD), SGD with momentum, Nesterov momentum, and Adam. It reaches equivalent test accuracies after the same number of training epochs, but with fewer parameter updates

cards.conditions: Interpreted from stochastic differential equation perspective; applies to SGD variants
cards.effect: Predicts equivalence of learning rate decay and batch size increase; optimal batch size proportional to learning rate
cards.evidence: Theoretical analysis citing Smith & Le (2017); validated empirically across optimizer types on CIFAR-10
cards.quote: They also proved that the "noise scale" , where is the learning rate, the training set size and the batch size. This noise scale controls the magnitude of the random fluctuations in the training dynamics... we may achieve the same reduction in noise scale at constant learning rate by increasing the batch size

cards.claim: Linear scaling rule: batch size increase requires proportional learning rate increase to maintain convergence
cards.conditions: SGD with momentum on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet; up to batch size = training set size
cards.effect: Enables large batch training (8192→81920 on ImageNet) without hyperparameter search
cards.evidence: Empirical validation across CIFAR-10 and ImageNet experiments; cited prior work (Goyal et al. 2017, Krizhevsky 2014)
cards.quote: Goyal et al. (2017) exploited a linear scaling rule between batch size and learning rate to train ResNet-50 on ImageNet in one hour with batches of 8192 images... we repurpose existing training schedules for large batch training with no hyper-parameter tuning

cards.claim: Small batch training generalizes better than large batch training (generalization gap); optimal batch size maximizes test accuracy at constant learning rate
cards.conditions: SGD family optimizers; CIFAR-10 and ImageNet tasks
cards.effect: Trade-off: larger batch sizes reduce parameter updates but may reduce generalization if noise scale not properly maintained
cards.evidence: Literature review (Keskar et al. 2016) and empirical observation; Smith & Le (2017) identified optimal batch size linked to optimal noise scale
cards.quote: To the surprise of many researchers, it is now increasingly accepted that small batch training often generalizes better to the test set than large batch training. This "generalization gap" was explored extensively by Keskar et al. (2016). Smith & Le (2017) observed an optimal batch size which maximized the test set accuracy at constant learning rate. They argued that this optimal batch size arises when the noise scale is also optimal

cards.claim: Increasing momentum coefficient with batch size increases per-example update suppression timescale; accumulation forgets old gradients over ~μ/(1-μ) epochs
cards.conditions: SGD with momentum on CIFAR-10; momentum coefficient increased from 0.9 to 0.98 while scaling batch size
cards.effect: Slight accuracy reduction when momentum increased (94.2% → 93.3% on CIFAR-10); accumulation cannot adapt to loss landscape changes if timescale exceeds several epochs
cards.evidence: Theoretical analysis (Appendix A) and experimental ablation; comparison of four schedules with increasing momentum (0.9, 0.95, 0.975, 0.9875)
cards.quote: Furthermore, when we increase the momentum coefficient we increase the timescale required for the accumulation to forget old gradients (this timescale is also ). Once this timescale becomes several epochs long, the accumulation cannot adapt to changes in the loss landscape, impeding training. This is likely to be particularly problematic at points where the noise scale decays

cards.claim: Increasing initial learning rate and scaling batch size reduces parameter updates substantially; initial LR up to 0.4-0.5 maintains accuracy on CIFAR-10
cards.conditions: Wide ResNet on CIFAR-10; 50000 training images; batch size up to 6400 (1/8 of training set); fixed epoch budget (200 epochs)
cards.effect: Test accuracy maintained at ~94.2-94.5% while reducing updates from 80,000 to 6,500; above LR~0.4 accuracy falls
cards.evidence: Experimental comparison of four schedules with increasing LR (0.1→0.5) and varying initial batch sizes; Appendix B systematic LR sweep
cards.quote: We show here that we can also increase the effective learning rate at the start of training, while scaling the initial batch size. All experiments are conducted using SGD with momentum... 'Increased initial learning rate' requires under 6500 updates, reaching a final accuracy of 94.5%. We find that the test accuracy falls for initial learning rates larger than 0.4

cards.claim: Ghost batch normalization (with fixed ghost batch size) prevents mean gradient dependency on actual batch size, enabling noise-scale-based scaling
cards.conditions: Wide ResNet on CIFAR-10; ghost batch norm with ghost batch size 128 (constant) while actual batch size varies
cards.effect: Ensures equivalence between LR decay and batch size increase; decouples BN statistics from batch size effects
cards.evidence: Methodology cited from Hoffer et al. (2017); applied in CIFAR-10 experiments to satisfy Smith & Le (2017) analysis requirements
cards.quote: We use ghost batch norm ( Hoffer et al., 2017 ) , with a ghost batch size of 128. This ensures the mean gradient is independent of batch size, as required by the analysis of Smith & Le (2017)

cards.claim: At maximum batch size (= training set size or hardware limit), revert to learning rate decay rather than further batch size increases
cards.conditions: ImageNet with Inception-ResNet-V2; training set 1.28M images; batch size saturates at hardware/memory limit (81920 on TPU)
cards.effect: Maintains noise scale decay trajectory; prevents exceeding optimal batch size which would reduce generalization
cards.evidence: ImageNet experiments Section 5.3-5.4; practical observation that hardware constraints force switch at β_max
cards.quote: The main contribution of this work is to show that it is possible to make efficient use of vast training batches, if one increases the batch size during training at constant learning rate until . After this point, we revert to the use of decaying learning rates
